title: Pascal's night of fire
hook: on 23 November 1654, Pascal writes two hours of fire on paper and sews it into his coat (the Memorial)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis and the wolf, and a peace that fed a hungry creature. Your line was brother wolf. Did you ask what someone was hungry for? Day ninety.

Is there something you keep close without telling anyone? A note from someone who's gone, folded in your wallet. A screenshot you never delete. A ticket stub in a drawer. Small things, the kind people say they'd run back into a burning house for. Way back on day two, we met Blaise Pascal, who said our unhappiness comes from not being able to sit quietly in a room. Today we find out what happened to him one night, alone in his own room, and what, the story goes, he carried in his coat from then on. Today's story is Pascal's night of fire.
screen: `A NOTE IN YOUR WALLET.` → `PASCAL, BACK FROM DAY TWO.` → `ONE NIGHT, ALONE IN HIS ROOM.`

segments.voice: Pascal was a mathematician and an inventor. And on a Monday night, the twenty-third of November, 1654, something happened to him, from about half past ten until about half past midnight. We don't know exactly what. What we have is what he wrote down, right then, on a sheet of paper. It starts with a date and a time. Then one word, in capital letters: fire. Then he wrote that the God he met that night was the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob, and not the God of the philosophers and the scholars. This from a philosopher and scholar. Then, in broken lines, like someone out of breath: certainty; feeling; joy; peace. And the word joy, three times over, and tears of joy. He never published it, and as far as we know he never spoke of it. The story told after his death is that it was found sewn into the lining of his coat, when a servant felt something stiff there, and that he had moved it by hand each time he changed coats. It's called the Memorial. For Pascal it was a meeting with God, the heart of his Christian faith. For anyone, it's a picture of how to treat the few moments that matter most. Not as content to post. As something to keep close.
screen: `A MATHEMATICIAN AND INVENTOR.` · `23 NOVEMBER 1654: FIRE.` · `NOT THE GOD OF THE PHILOSOPHERS.` · `SEWN INTO HIS COAT.` · then, large: `KEEP IT CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write one line you want to keep. Settle, and breathe. Think back over your life for a moment that mattered: a night, a sentence someone said, a place where something became clear. Don't pick the most dramatic; pick the truest. Find the fewest words that hold it. Maybe just a date and one word, like Pascal's. After the bell, if you like, write it down on a small piece of paper and put it somewhere close: a wallet, a pocket, a phone case. The bell holds the time.
Pascal's night of fire. Two hours in 1654 that he wrote on a single page, sewed into his coat, and carried unseen until he died. Today's word.
Your line: keep it close. Today, carry your line with you somewhere nobody sees, and touch it once when the day gets loud. Day ninety.

howItsDone: Christians who read Pascal treasure the Memorial as the record of his encounter with God; some people keep a copy of it, or a line of their own, close at hand in the same spirit.

fork.setup: you're Pascal. you've just lived two hours you can barely put into words, and you've written them on a single page. what do you do with it?
options: publish it in your next book
sew it into the lining of your coat
burn it, so no one misreads it
fork.reveal: the story told after his death is that he sewed it into his coat and moved it to each new one. a servant found it there.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mathematician had a strange night.
what it means: the moment that mattered most, kept close and private, not shown off.
what a scholar hears: the Memorial dates itself: Monday, 23 November 1654, from about half past ten at night until about half past midnight.

notes: The Memorial is described and paraphrased, not quoted (Trotter 1910 is on the list, but its rendering of the Memorial was not certain). Confirm: date and times (about 10:30 pm to 12:30 am), the heading FEU, God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob not of the philosophers and scholars, certainty, feeling, joy, peace, tears of joy.
Found after his death (August 1662) sewn into his coat, discovered by a servant; the parchment original with a paper draft: confirm.

Pascal's calculator (the Pascaline, built from about age 19), probability correspondence with Fermat (1654), the SI unit pascal: confirm. 'As a teenager' may be a stretch if the first model dates to age 19–20.
'Never told anyone, as far as we know': confirm.

Editor review (days 76-94 pass): cut the superlatives and unsourced facts (sharpest minds, teenage calculator, Fermat, the pascal unit, age thirty-one, eight years, 1662, parchment copy); the date and hours stay because the Memorial states them; the coat and servant are now 'the story told after his death' in teach, myth and fork; hook no longer tells the listener what they would do.
